articles.title: TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface
articles.description: Modern tuple types deliver position-based safety, labeled elements for IDE clarity, and variadic spreads for function composition. Learn when tuples beat interfaces and when to walk away.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most TypeScript engineers reach for interfaces when they need structured data. That reflex breaks when an API returns coordinates, a useState hook returns [value, setter], or middleware needs to compose through a chain of handlers. Arrays do not enforce length or per-index types. Interfaces force named property access when destructuring is cleaner.

The type system accepts [string, number] as valid but offers no hints at the call site. Engineers write result[0] with no indication whether zero holds a user ID or an error message. The compiler stays silent when position assumptions drift.

Labeled tuple elements fix this. The syntax [id: string, count: number] preserves position semantics while surfacing parameter names in autocomplete and signature help. Variadic tuple types compose middleware signatures. Readonly tuples prevent mutation.

The mechanics have been in TypeScript since 4.0 (August 2020) with variadic tuples and 4.2 (February 2021) with leading/trailing rest elements, per the TypeScript 4.0 release notes and 4.2 release notes. By 2026 the patterns are stable. What remains is knowing when a tuple wins over an interface and when adding a fourth element means you picked the wrong tool.

Key Takeaways

  • Labeled tuple elements [id: string, count: number] surface parameter names in IDE autocomplete and signature help with zero runtime cost.
  • Variadic tuple types enable type-safe function composition and middleware pipelines by spreading rest parameters into tuple positions.
  • Tuples beat interfaces when destructuring order matters, when position carries semantic meaning, or when returning small fixed-length collections from functions.
  • Readonly tuples and as const assertions prevent runtime mutations and lock down literal types at compile time.
  • Long tuples (more than 4 elements) sacrifice readability; switch to an interface when named properties clarify intent better than position.

What Makes TypeScript Tuples Different From Arrays in 2026

A tuple enforces fixed length and per-index types; an array enforces element homogeneity across unknown length.

An array of numbers number[] accepts zero elements or a million. The type system cannot tell you what lives at index three. A tuple [string, number, boolean] must hold exactly three elements with those exact types at those exact positions.

// Array: homogeneous, variable length
const scores: number[] = [42, 97, 88];
scores.push(103); // valid
const first = scores[0]; // type: number | undefined

// Tuple: heterogeneous, fixed length
const user: [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
user.push(true); // error: Argument of type 'boolean' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string | number'
const name = user[0]; // type: string (exact)

The array allows mutation and length changes. The tuple enforces structure. When an API returns a latitude/longitude pair, [number, number] guarantees two elements. number[] leaves the consumer guessing whether the array holds two values or twenty.

Tuples compose with union types. A function returning [data: User, error: null] | [data: null, error: Error] models a result type with discriminated positions. The caller destructures and checks the second element to know whether the first element is valid.

function fetchUser(id: string): [data: User, error: null] | [data: null, error: Error] {
  // implementation
}

const [data, error] = fetchUser("123");
if (error) {
  console.error(error.message);
} else {
  console.log(data.name); // TypeScript knows data is User here
}

Arrays do not support this pattern. The type system cannot track which index holds the discriminant and which holds the payload. Tuples give you that precision.

TypeScript tuple type checking in IDE

Labeled Tuple Elements: Self-Documenting Types That Show Up in Your IDE

Labeled elements annotate each position with a parameter name, surfacing that name in IDE tooltips and autocomplete without changing the runtime shape.

The syntax [x: number, y: number] looks like a function signature. That is deliberate. When you destructure const [x, y] = getCoordinates(), the IDE shows those labels in the autocomplete list. The compiler still enforces position, not property access.

// Without labels
type Unlabeled = [number, number];
const point: Unlabeled = [10, 20];
// IDE shows: const point: [number, number]

// With labels
type Labeled = [x: number, y: number];
const labeledPoint: Labeled = [10, 20];
// IDE shows: const labeledPoint: [x: number, y: number]
// Destructuring autocomplete suggests 'x' and 'y'

Labels do not change destructuring semantics. You can still write const [a, b] = labeledPoint and a will hold the first element. Labels serve documentation, not enforcement. The compiler does not reject const [latitude, longitude] = labeledPoint even though the labels say x and y.

The real payoff comes in function signatures. A handler accepting (event: [type: string, payload: unknown]) => void shows those labels when you hover over the parameter. Compare that to (event: [string, unknown]) => void, which forces the reader to guess what the second element represents.

Labeled tuples pair well with utility types. A tuple [id: string, count: number] passed to Readonly<[id: string, count: number]> preserves labels while preventing mutation. The labels survive through type transformations.

Per the TypeScript 4.0 handbook on labeled tuple elements, labels must appear on all elements or none. Mixing labeled and unlabeled positions within the same tuple triggers a compiler error. Consistency keeps the intent clear.

Variadic Tuple Types: Composing Function Signatures and Middleware Pipelines

Variadic tuples spread rest parameters into fixed positions, enabling type-safe function composition and middleware stacks without manual overload declarations.

Before variadic tuples, composing two functions meant writing overloads for every arity. A pipe utility accepting (a: A) => B and (b: B) => C could not infer types for a third function without another overload. Variadic tuples solve this with spreads.

// A compose function that preserves types
type Fn<T extends unknown[], R> = (...args: T) => R;

function compose<A extends unknown[], B, C>(
  f: Fn<A, B>,
  g: Fn<[B], C>
): Fn<A, C> {
  return (...args: A) => g(f(...args));
}

const addOne = (x: number) => x + 1;
const toString = (n: number) => n.toString();

const addThenStringify = compose(addOne, toString);
const result = addThenStringify(5); // type: string, value: "6"

The A extends unknown[] parameter captures the first function's argument tuple. The return type Fn<A, C> spreads that same tuple into the composed function's signature. TypeScript infers A as [number] when you pass addOne, then enforces that the composed function accepts number.

Middleware pipelines benefit more. An HTTP handler chain starts with [req: Request, res: Response] and each middleware adds context. Variadic tuples let you compose handlers that append parameters without losing type safety.

type Handler<T extends unknown[]> = (...args: T) => void | Promise<void>;

function withAuth<T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]]>(
  next: Handler<T>
): Handler<T> {
  return async (...args: T) => {
    const [req] = args;
    // auth logic
    return next(...args);
  };
}

function withLogging<T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]]>(
  next: Handler<T>
): Handler<T> {
  return async (...args: T) => {
    const [req] = args;
    console.log(req.url);
    return next(...args);
  };
}

const baseHandler: Handler<[Request, Response]> = (req, res) => {
  res.send("OK");
};

const protected = withAuth(withLogging(baseHandler));
// Type inferred: Handler<[Request, Response]>

The T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]] constraint preserves the leading two elements and allows trailing additions. Each middleware wraps the next without breaking the type chain. The final handler still accepts [Request, Response].

Variadic tuples also model Promise.all correctly. The built-in Promise.all<T extends readonly unknown[]>(values: T): Promise<{ [K in keyof T]: Awaited<T[K]> }> uses variadic spreads to map each promise to its resolved type. You get Promise<[string, number]> from Promise.all([Promise.resolve("a"), Promise.resolve(1)]) instead of Promise<(string | number)[]>.

When a Tuple Beats an Interface: Position, Destructuring, and Performance

Tuples win when position carries meaning, destructuring is idiomatic, or the structure is small and temporary.

An interface forces named property access. A tuple lets you destructure in the parameter list or assignment. When a hook returns [state, setState], destructuring is idiomatic. Forcing { state, setState } adds noise.

// Tuple: destructure at call site
function useCounter(): [count: number, increment: () => void] {
  // implementation
}
const [count, increment] = useCounter();

// Interface: named access
interface CounterResult {
  count: number;
  increment: () => void;
}
function useCounterObj(): CounterResult {
  // implementation
}
const { count, increment } = useCounterObj();

Both work. The tuple version mirrors React's useState convention. The interface version clarifies when return values exceed two or three fields. Pick based on idiom and size.

Criterion Tuple Interface
Element count 2-4 elements 4+ fields
Destructuring const [a, b] = fn() const { a, b } = fn()
Property renaming Position-based, rename freely Must match property names or use alias
Documentation Labels in IDE, position implicit Property names explicit
Type overhead No keys, direct access Property lookup, structural check
Extension Cannot add optional trailing elements Can extend with optional properties

Tuples avoid property name collisions. When merging two results, destructuring with different names is trivial: const [user, setUser] = useUser(); const [post, setPost] = usePost();. Interfaces require renaming: const { data: userData } = fetchUser(); const { data: postData } = fetchPost();.

Performance differences are negligible. Both compile to arrays or objects. Tuples carry less metadata at runtime (no property keys), but modern engines optimize both paths. Choose based on semantics, not speed.

Tuples also model discriminated unions compactly. A result type [ok: true, data: T] | [ok: false, error: Error] discriminates on the first element. Interfaces would need a separate status field and duplicate the discriminant check.

Readonly Tuples and as const: Preventing Mutations at Compile Time

Readonly tuples block push, pop, and index assignment; as const assertions lock down literal types and infer readonly tuples automatically.

A bare tuple [string, number] allows mutation. The compiler accepts tuple[0] = "new value" and tuple.push(42) (though push violates the fixed length, the runtime allows it). Wrapping in Readonly<...> or using readonly [string, number] prevents both.

// Mutable tuple
const mutable: [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
mutable[0] = "Bob"; // allowed
mutable.push(100); // runtime error, but TypeScript allows it

// Readonly tuple
const immutable: readonly [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
immutable[0] = "Bob"; // error: Index signature in type 'readonly [string, number]' only permits reading
immutable.push(100); // error: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly [string, number]'

The readonly modifier removes push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, and index assignment. The tuple becomes a pure value. Functions accepting readonly [string, number] signal they will not mutate the input.

The as const assertion infers readonly tuples and narrows literals to their exact values. Without it, TypeScript widens ["Alice", 29] to (string | number)[]. With it, the type becomes readonly ["Alice", 29] with literal types.

// Without as const
const widened = ["Alice", 29]; // type: (string | number)[]

// With as const
const narrowed = ["Alice", 29] as const; // type: readonly ["Alice", 29]
const name = narrowed[0]; // type: "Alice" (literal)
const age = narrowed[1]; // type: 29 (literal)

This pairs well with exhaustive checks. A tuple ["success", "error", "pending"] as const gives you a union "success" | "error" | "pending" when spread. The compiler ensures switch statements cover all three cases.

const statuses = ["success", "error", "pending"] as const;
type Status = typeof statuses[number]; // "success" | "error" | "pending"

function handleStatus(status: Status) {
  switch (status) {
    case "success":
      return "OK";
    case "error":
      return "Failed";
    case "pending":
      return "Loading";
    default:
      const _exhaustive: never = status; // compiler error if a case is missing
      return _exhaustive;
  }
}

Readonly tuples prevent a class of bugs where shared state mutates unexpectedly. When a function returns readonly [User, Metadata], callers cannot accidentally modify the cached result. The type system enforces immutability without defensive copying.

Per the TypeScript handbook on const assertions, as const applies recursively. A nested tuple [["a", 1], ["b", 2]] as const becomes readonly [readonly ["a", 1], readonly ["b", 2]]. All layers lock down.

TypeScript readonly tuple preventing mutations

Real-World Patterns: API Returns, Event Handlers, and Multi-Value State

Tuples model API results with error/data pairs, event payloads with type and data, and stateful hooks returning value and setter.

A common pattern wraps API calls in a result tuple. The first element holds data on success, null on error. The second element holds the error or null. Destructuring gives immediate access to both.

async function fetchUserSafe(id: string): Promise<[data: User | null, error: Error | null]> {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    const user = await response.json();
    return [user, null];
  } catch (err) {
    return [null, err instanceof Error ? err : new Error(String(err))];
  }
}

const [user, error] = await fetchUserSafe("123");
if (error) {
  console.error("Failed to fetch user:", error.message);
} else {
  console.log("User:", user.name);
}

The caller checks the error element first. If null, the data element is safe to use. If present, the data element is null. The type system enforces this through union narrowing. No try/catch block needed at the call site.

Event handlers in frameworks like Svelte or custom event systems use tuples to pair event type with payload. A handler signature (event: [type: "click", target: HTMLElement]) => void documents both fields.

type ClickEvent = [type: "click", target: HTMLElement];
type KeyEvent = [type: "keydown", key: string];
type AppEvent = ClickEvent | KeyEvent;

function handleEvent(event: AppEvent) {
  const [type, payload] = event;
  if (type === "click") {
    console.log("Clicked:", payload.tagName);
  } else {
    console.log("Key pressed:", payload);
  }
}

The discriminant lives in the first position. TypeScript narrows payload based on type. A union of labeled tuples models tagged unions compactly.

Stateful hooks return tuples to mirror React conventions. A custom useToggle hook returns [value: boolean, toggle: () => void]. The caller destructures with meaningful names: const [isOpen, toggleOpen] = useToggle(false).

function useToggle(initial: boolean): [value: boolean, toggle: () => void] {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(initial);
  const toggle = () => setValue(v => !v);
  return [value, toggle];
}

Tuples keep the return compact. An interface would force { value, toggle }, which adds boilerplate. The tuple version reads cleaner when composing multiple hooks in a component.

For more on validating complex structures, see our guide on TypeScript form validators and custom validation logic, which covers zod and yup integration.

Common Pitfalls: Long Tuples, Type Inference Traps, and When to Use Objects Instead

Tuples lose clarity beyond four elements, inference fails when types are too similar, and objects win when order is arbitrary.

A tuple with six elements becomes unreadable. [string, number, boolean, string, Date, null] forces the reader to count positions. Named properties clarify intent faster than position.

// Bad: long tuple
type UserData = [id: string, name: string, age: number, email: string, createdAt: Date, deletedAt: Date | null];

// Better: interface
interface UserData {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  age: number;
  email: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  deletedAt: Date | null;
}

The interface version documents each field. The tuple version hides meaning behind indices. When you need more than four elements, switch to an object.

Type inference struggles when adjacent elements share types. A function returning [string, string] gives no hint which string holds the user ID and which holds the display name. Labels help, but the compiler cannot enforce destructuring order.

function getUser(): [id: string, name: string] {
  return ["u123", "Alice"];
}

const [name, id] = getUser(); // swapped, but compiler allows it

The destructured variables have the right types (both string), but the semantics are wrong. The compiler cannot catch this. When adjacent elements share types, consider an interface or an object with distinct keys.

Optional trailing elements create inference ambiguity. A tuple [string, number?] can hold one or two elements. Destructuring const [a, b] = tuple gives a: string and b: number | undefined, but you cannot tell from the type whether the tuple had one element or two.

type OptionalTuple = [name: string, age?: number];

const single: OptionalTuple = ["Alice"];
const double: OptionalTuple = ["Bob", 30];

const [name1, age1] = single; // age1: number | undefined
const [name2, age2] = double; // age2: number | undefined

The type system cannot distinguish at the call site. If the presence of the second element matters, model it as a discriminated union: [name: string] | [name: string, age: number].

Tuples also fail when order is arbitrary. A coordinate pair [x: number, y: number] has semantic order (horizontal, vertical). A user record with [email: string, phone: string] does not. Which comes first is a convention, not a constraint. Use an interface when order is arbitrary.

For a deeper dive into advanced type constraints, see our post on TypeScript generic constraints with extends and keyof.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should you use a labeled tuple instead of an interface?

Use a labeled tuple when the structure has 2-4 elements with semantic position order and the consumer will destructure it. Examples include coordinate pairs [x: number, y: number], React hook returns [state: T, setState: (val: T) => void], or result tuples [data: T | null, error: Error | null]. Use an interface when the structure exceeds four fields, when property names clarify intent better than position, or when order is arbitrary.

How do variadic tuple types improve function composition?

Variadic tuple types spread rest parameters into fixed positions, letting you compose functions without manual overloads. A compose utility can preserve the first function's argument tuple through type inference: compose<A extends unknown[], B, C>(f: (...args: A) => B, g: (b: B) => C): (...args: A) => C. The type system infers A from the first function and applies it to the composed result, maintaining type safety across the chain.

What happens when you use as const on a tuple literal?

The as const assertion infers a readonly tuple with literal types for each element. ["Alice", 29] as const becomes readonly ["Alice", 29] with types "Alice" and 29 instead of string and number. The readonly modifier prevents mutation, and the literal types enable exhaustive checking in discriminated unions. The assertion applies recursively to nested structures.

Can you extend a tuple type with additional elements?

TypeScript supports optional trailing elements with ? syntax: [required: string, optional?: number]. You cannot extend a named tuple type with inheritance the way you extend interfaces. Variadic tuple types allow composition: type Extended<T extends unknown[]> = [...T, extra: boolean] appends an element to the end. For dynamic extension, use rest elements: [first: string, ...rest: number[]].

When does a tuple perform better than an interface?

Tuples and interfaces both compile to runtime arrays or objects, and modern JavaScript engines optimize both paths aggressively. Tuples carry slightly less metadata (no property keys), but the performance difference is negligible in practice. Choose tuples for semantic reasons (position matters, destructuring is idiomatic) rather than performance. Microbenchmarks may show tiny differences, but they vanish under real workload variance.

Tuples in 2026: What You Should Reach For and When to Walk Away

Tuples deliver position-based type safety when destructuring is idiomatic and structure is small. Labeled elements clarify intent without runtime cost. Variadic spreads compose function signatures cleanly. Readonly tuples prevent mutation.

The pattern breaks at five elements. When property names clarify better than position, an interface wins. When adjacent elements share types, the compiler cannot catch swapped destructuring. When order is arbitrary, forcing a tuple sacrifices clarity for no gain.

Reach for tuples when returning small fixed-length collections from functions, modeling discriminated unions compactly, or composing middleware pipelines. Walk away when the structure grows past four fields, when naming beats numbering, or when the caller does not destructure. The type system gives you both tools. Use the one that documents intent.

For further refinement of type utilities, explore our coverage of Partial, Required, and DeepPartial patterns in TypeScript.

articles.body_html:
Description: Python security, screen capture, spring physics, HiDPI and PyInstaller .exe gotchas. 7 tests from shipping 3 no-telemetry Python apps for Windows (ATLOCK, ASNIPP, APIC).

Most Python developers can write a for loop, a Flask route and a pandas one-liner.

Python experts know what happens before line 1 runs, what Python can't do, and what breaks the moment your script leaves your laptop.

I found out which one I was while building three Windows desktop apps in pure Python: ATLOCK (a security suite), ASNIPP (a screenshot and screen recorder) and APIC (an image toolkit). No ads, no analytics SDKs, no bloat. Every test below is a real bug or design decision from one of them.

Score yourself honestly. 👇

Test 1: Do you know that import order can be a security decision? (ATLOCK)

Quick: what does import ctypes have to do with security?

On Windows, a DLL imported later can be loaded from the current directory. That is how DLL planting attacks work. The fix has to run before the other imports:

import sys, ctypes

if sys.platform == "win32":
    k32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)
    k32.SetDllDirectoryW.argtypes = [ctypes.c_wchar_p]
    k32.SetDllDirectoryW("")                      # drop the CWD from the DLL search path
    k32.SetDefaultDllDirectories.argtypes = [ctypes.c_uint32]
    k32.SetDefaultDllDirectories(0x1000)          # LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS

# only NOW import the heavy stuff
import cryptography, argon2

Developer: puts imports in alphabetical order.
Expert: knows import order is a runtime security boundary.

This is the very first thing that runs in ATLOCK, my pure-Python security suite.

Test 2: Can your screen recorder avoid recording itself? (ASNIPP)

I built a screen recorder with a floating control bar. First recording: the bar showed up in the video. 🤦

You don't need to hide and show windows. One Win32 call, straight from Python, does it:

import ctypes

def exclude_from_capture(widget):
    hwnd = int(widget.winId())
    # 0x11 = WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE (Windows 10 2004+)
    ctypes.windll.user32.SetWindowDisplayAffinity(hwnd, 0x11)

The window stays visible to you and is invisible to every screen capture. That is how ASNIPP keeps its own toolbars, drawing overlay and recording border out of your videos.

Developer: crops the bar out in post.
Expert: knows ctypes gives Python the whole Windows API.

Test 3: Can your app decide what you meant, without asking? (APIC)

Good desktop software removes clicks. In APIC, my image toolkit, the rule is simple:

  • Drop one image → open it in the editor.
  • Drop many → open the batch converter. 
def on_files(self, paths: list[str]):
    if not paths:
        paths, _ = QFileDialog.getOpenFileNames(
            self, "Open Image(s)", "",
            "Images (*.png *.jpg *.jpeg *.webp *.bmp *.tiff *.gif *.ico *.heic *.avif)")
    if len(paths) == 1:
        self.open_in_edit(paths[0])
    elif paths:
        self.open_in_convert(paths)

def dropEvent(self, event):
    self.on_files([u.toLocalFile() for u in event.mimeData().urls()])

The home screen, the file dialog and drag-and-drop all go through one function. Add a new entry point and you add zero logic.

Developer: writes three code paths.
Expert: writes one funnel and lets every input flow into it. The UI is split into one module per mode (edit, convert, compress, search), and main.py only wires them together.

Test 4: Do you know the difference between "encrypted" and "encrypted correctly"? (ATLOCK)

Developer: AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB) and done.

Expert checklist:

  • AEAD, not just encryption: AES-256-GCM authenticates every chunk.
  • Slow KDF for passwords: Argon2id, not a bare SHA-256.
  • Never reuse a nonce with the same key.
  • Bind the header with AAD so metadata can't be swapped. 
import os
from argon2.low_level import hash_secret_raw, Type
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

def seal(password: bytes, data: bytes) -> bytes:
    salt = os.urandom(16)
    key = hash_secret_raw(password, salt, time_cost=3, memory_cost=64 * 1024,
                          parallelism=4, hash_len=32, type=Type.ID)
    nonce = os.urandom(12)
    ct = AESGCM(key).encrypt(nonce, data, associated_data=b"v1")
    return salt + nonce + ct

(Simplified. ATLOCK's real container format also does chunking, key commitment and versioning.)

Test 5: Can you make a Qt animation feel alive with 6 lines of math? (ASNIPP)

ASNIPP's capture bar is a "Dynamic Island" that bounces open. Qt's built-in easing curves felt stiff, so I wrote a damped spring and plugged it into QEasingCurve:

import math
from PyQt6.QtCore import QEasingCurve

def spring(zeta, omega):
    wd = omega * math.sqrt(max(1e-6, 1 - zeta * zeta)) if zeta < 1 else 0.0
    def f(t):
        if t <= 0: return 0.0
        if t >= 1: return 1.0
        if zeta < 1:    # under-damped: overshoots, then settles (the bounce)
            return 1 - math.exp(-zeta * omega * t) * (math.cos(wd * t) + (zeta * omega / wd) * math.sin(wd * t))
        return 1 - math.exp(-omega * t) * (1 + omega * t)   # critically damped: no overshoot
    return f

BOUNCY = spring(0.66, 11.0)   # keep it at MODULE level (see below)

curve = QEasingCurve(QEasingCurve.Type.Linear)
curve.setCustomType(BOUNCY)

The trap: if the function is a temporary object, Python garbage-collects it while Qt still holds a pointer, and you get random crashes. Keep custom callables alive at module level. Only people who've been bitten know this one.

Test 6: Does your app look sharp on a 4K laptop with 150% scaling? (APIC)

Most Python GUI apps look blurry or oddly sized on modern displays. In Qt 6 the fix is one policy before you create the app:

from PyQt6.QtWidgets import QApplication
from PyQt6.QtCore import Qt

QApplication.setHighDpiScaleFactorRoundingPolicy(
    Qt.HighDpiScaleFactorRoundingPolicy.PassThrough)   # no rounding: 125%/150% stay crisp

app = QApplication(sys.argv)
app.setApplicationName("APIC")
app.setOrganizationName("Akhouri Systems")

PassThrough keeps fractional scales like 125% and 150% exact instead of snapping to 100% or 200%. Add one try/except AttributeError for older Qt builds, and your app looks native everywhere.

Developer: tests on their own monitor.
Expert: tests at 100%, 125%, 150% and 200%.

Test 7: Can you explain why Python can't truly erase a password from memory? (ATLOCK) 

password = "hunter2"
password = None   # is it gone? 🙂

No. Python str and bytes are immutable, and the interpreter is free to copy them. The best you can do is keep secrets in a mutable bytearray and wipe it explicitly:

buf = bytearray(b"hunter2")
# ... use it ...
for i in range(len(buf)):
    buf[i] = 0

An honest Python security tool says this out loud instead of promising magic. ATLOCK's source header lists what it can't do: memory wiping is best-effort, SSD shredding can't be guaranteed, and a same-user attacker can modify the script. Python experts document their limits.

Bonus: "Why does it work in VS Code and silently do nothing as a .exe?"

All three of my apps ship as Python compiled with PyInstaller (--onefile --windowed). It cost me an evening before I learned this: in a windowed build, sys.stdout and sys.stderr are None. Any print(), logging call or library traceback can fail silently, and your app "just doesn't open."

import sys, os

for name in ("stdout", "stderr"):
    if getattr(sys, name, None) is None:
        setattr(sys, name, open(os.devnull, "w", encoding="utf-8"))

# and show errors somewhere a human can see them:
import ctypes
ctypes.windll.user32.MessageBoxW(None, "Startup failed: ...", "App error", 0x10)

Try the code yourself

I'm the developer behind all of this, and the three apps are the proof that it works outside tutorials. They're built by Akhouri Systems, each is pure Python packaged as an .exe in a zip, with no ads and no analytics. The only network features are the ones you trigger yourself (for example ATLOCK's optional breach check, which sends only a 5-character hash prefix).

App Python lesson it proves What it is Get it
🔐 ATLOCK v5 Tests 1, 4, 7 Security suite: AES-256-GCM + Argon2id file guard, password vault, TOTP/FIDO2, anti-tamper Direct download (zip) · Microsoft Store
📸 ASNIPP v1 Tests 2, 5 Dynamic-Island-style screenshot, screen recorder, live drawing and editor Direct download (zip)
🖼️ APIC v1 Tests 3, 6 Image edit, convert, compress and search toolkit Direct download (zip)

If you're learning how Python behaves outside a notebook, run them and then ask what's going on under the hood. That's the fastest way I know to level up.

Your score

  • 0–2 tests known: You're a Python developer. Great start, now go break things.
  • 3–5: Solid. You've shipped something real.
  • 6–7: You're a Python expert. Come argue with me in the comments.

Which test did you fail first? Mine was the windowed-.exe one, and I lost an entire evening to it. Tell me yours below 👇

articles.title: How I finally understood the Dependency Inversion Principle
articles.description: The Intro   Last stop. We made it to the D: the Dependency Inversion Principle.  This one is...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Last stop. We made it to the D: the Dependency Inversion Principle.

This one is special because the other four kind of lead here. SRP gave us small classes. OCP taught us to add instead of edit. LSP and ISP gave us honest, tiny interfaces. DIP is where we decide who points at whom.

Buckle up, it's the one that changes how your main.ts looks forever.

The What

The definition has two parts:

High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.

Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions.

Four sentences that use "depend" five times. Cool cool cool.

Plain version: your business logic should not import your database driver. The important stuff (orders, invoices, rules) should sit at the top and know nothing about the plumbing (Postgres, Stripe, the file system). The plumbing should plug into the business logic, not the other way around.

Let's build an order checkout and watch the arrows flip.

The How

Here is OrderService, the "high-level" part of our store. It's the thing that knows what placing an order means:

// src/order-service.ts
import { PostgresOrderRepository } from './postgres-order-repository.js'
import { StripeClient } from './stripe-client.js'

export class OrderService {
  private readonly orders = new PostgresOrderRepository('postgres://localhost/shop')
  private readonly stripe = new StripeClient(process.env.STRIPE_KEY!)

  async placeOrder(customerId: string, total: number) {
    await this.stripe.charge(customerId, total)
    const id = await this.orders.insert({ customerId, total })
    console.log(`🧾 order ${id} placed`)
    return id
  }
}

The two "low-level" pieces:

// src/postgres-order-repository.ts
export class PostgresOrderRepository {
  constructor(private readonly url: string) {}

  async insert(order: { customerId: string; total: number }) {
    console.log(`🐘 INSERT INTO orders ... (${this.url})`)
    return 'ord_123'
  }
}

// src/stripe-client.ts
export class StripeClient {
  constructor(private readonly apiKey: string) {}

  async charge(customerId: string, amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 stripe charged ${customerId} $${amount}`)
  }
}

And main:

// src/main.ts
import { OrderService } from './order-service.js'

await new OrderService().placeOrder('cus_42', 99)

Run it, it works, everyone goes home. 🏠

Now draw the arrows. Who imports whom?

OrderService  ──▶  PostgresOrderRepository
OrderService  ──▶  StripeClient

The most important class in the app depends on the two most replaceable classes in the app. That's upside down. And here's how you feel it:

  • Want to write a test for placeOrder()? Congratulations, your test now needs a running Postgres and a Stripe API key. For a function with two lines of logic.
  • Marketing wants a free-trial checkout with no payment? You're going to put an if inside OrderService to skip Stripe. Then another for the sandbox. Then...
  • The database team migrates to MySQL? Open OrderService, the one file that should never care.
  • Running it locally charges a real card if STRIPE_KEY is a real key. Ask me how I know. 😬

The service news its own dependencies, so it is welded to them. Let's cut the welds.

Step 1: the high-level module describes what it needs

OrderService needs two things: somewhere to put orders, and something that can take money. It should describe those in its own words, not in Postgres or Stripe words:

// src/order-service.ts
export interface NewOrder {
  customerId: string
  total: number
}

export interface OrderRepository {
  insert(order: NewOrder): Promise<string>
}

export interface PaymentGateway {
  charge(customerId: string, amount: number): Promise<void>
}

export class OrderService {
  constructor(
    private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
    private readonly payments: PaymentGateway,
  ) {}

  async placeOrder(customerId: string, total: number) {
    await this.payments.charge(customerId, total)
    const id = await this.orders.insert({ customerId, total })
    console.log(`🧾 order ${id} placed`)
    return id
  }
}

Two things to notice:

  1. The interfaces live next to the service, because the service owns them. It says "this is what I need". That's the "abstractions belong to the high level" part.
  2. The dependencies come in through the constructor. The service doesn't build them anymore. That's the "dependency injection" part, which is the everyday tool we use to follow DIP.

Step 2: the details plug in 

// src/postgres-order-repository.ts
import type { OrderRepository, NewOrder } from './order-service.js'

export class PostgresOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
  constructor(private readonly url: string) {}

  async insert(order: NewOrder) {
    console.log(`🐘 INSERT INTO orders ... (${this.url})`)
    return 'ord_123'
  }
}

// src/stripe-payment-gateway.ts
import type { PaymentGateway } from './order-service.js'

export class StripePaymentGateway implements PaymentGateway {
  constructor(private readonly apiKey: string) {}

  async charge(customerId: string, amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 stripe charged ${customerId} $${amount}`)
  }
}

Look at the imports now. The Postgres class imports from order-service.ts. The arrow flipped:

PostgresOrderRepository  ──▶  OrderRepository (owned by OrderService)
StripePaymentGateway     ──▶  PaymentGateway  (owned by OrderService)

The plumbing points at the business logic. That's the "inversion".

Step 3: main.ts becomes the only place that knows everything 

// src/main.ts
import { OrderService } from './order-service.js'
import { PostgresOrderRepository } from './postgres-order-repository.js'
import { StripePaymentGateway } from './stripe-payment-gateway.js'

const service = new OrderService(
  new PostgresOrderRepository('postgres://localhost/shop'),
  new StripePaymentGateway(process.env.STRIPE_KEY!),
)

await service.placeOrder('cus_42', 99)

Same output as before. But now the big one: let's write that test.

Step 4: the test that used to be impossible 

// src/order-service.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest'
import { OrderService, type OrderRepository, type PaymentGateway } from './order-service.js'

class InMemoryOrders implements OrderRepository {
  saved: unknown[] = []
  async insert(order: unknown) {
    this.saved.push(order)
    return 'ord_test'
  }
}

class FakePayments implements PaymentGateway {
  charged: number[] = []
  async charge(_customerId: string, amount: number) {
    this.charged.push(amount)
  }
}

test('placing an order charges and saves it', async () => {
  const orders = new InMemoryOrders()
  const payments = new FakePayments()
  const service = new OrderService(orders, payments)

  const id = await service.placeOrder('cus_42', 99)

  expect(id).toBe('ord_test')
  expect(payments.charged).toEqual([99])
  expect(orders.saved).toHaveLength(1)
})

No Postgres. No Stripe. No mocking library. Two tiny classes that implement the interfaces OrderService asked for, and a test that runs in a millisecond.

And the free-trial checkout from earlier? new OrderService(repo, new NoChargeGateway()). Zero ifs inside the service.

The Why

Let's land this plane:

  • Business logic is the stable part; vendors are the volatile part. Stable code should never import volatile code. DIP is just that sentence turned into a rule.
  • Interfaces belong to the consumer. OrderService wrote PaymentGateway in its own vocabulary. Stripe adapted to it, not the other way around. When you swap Stripe for something else, the interface doesn't move.
  • Construction happens at the edge. main.ts (or your DI container, or your framework's wiring) is the only place that says new PostgresOrderRepository(...). Everything inside is handed what it needs.
  • Testing is a side effect, not a goal. We didn't "design for testability". We pointed the arrows the right way and the tests became easy on their own.

If you read my loosely coupled modules post, this should feel familiar. Same move, now with a name and a letter.

The Goodbye

And that's SOLID, all five letters, five tiny projects, five things we broke on purpose. If I had to compress the series into one line:

Small honest pieces, pointed at abstractions, glued together at the front door.

Thanks for riding along. Now go find a new keyword inside a service class and ask it why it's there. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: Durable execution for local LLM workflows: what I’m learning
articles.description: Most LLM demos assume the process stays alive. Kill it midway and the plan, the tool results, and the...
articles.body_html:
Most LLM demos assume the process stays alive. Kill it midway and the plan, the tool results, and the context all go with it. I've been spending time with a few tools that change that, and this is what I've picked up.

Durable execution changes how you think about failure

Temporal records every step of a workflow in an event history. If a worker dies, another one replays that history and continues from the last completed step. Finished work doesn't run twice.

For LLM workflows this maps well:

  • Model and tool calls belong in activities. They're slow, non-deterministic, and can fail, which is what activities are for.
  • Workflow code has to stay deterministic. Replay depends on it, so randomness, network calls, and timestamps stay out of it.
  • Retries become policy, not code. Backoff and timeouts are configuration instead of nested try/catch blocks.

Local models make failure cheap to test

Running a model through Ollama keeps the loop on your own machine. No rate limits, no API bill, and killing a process mid-run costs nothing. That makes it easy to test the unhappy path often, which is where most of the real bugs are.

The trade-off is that small local models are less predictable than hosted ones. Durable execution helps here because a bad step can be retried or inspected without redoing the whole run.

You can't trust what you can't see

Retries and resumes are invisible by default, and invisible failures are the hardest to debug. Sentry's tracing is a good fit, since a trace per step shows which call was slow, which one retried, and where a run picked back up.

A small React dashboard on top of the workflow history makes this easier still. Seeing a run's attempts as a timeline beats reading logs.

Open questions I'm still working through

  • How much state can sit in workflow history before replay gets slow?
  • Which failures should resume, and which should stop the run?
  • Does durability change how you write prompts and tool definitions?

I'll share more as I find answers.

articles.body_html:
Day 28 of 30 Days of Search.

Delete a photo. Close a tab you never saved. Uninstall an app.

The photo disappears, the tab comes back, and the app might remember your preferences when you reinstall it. None of those outcomes tells you, on its own, what happened to the data.

You can investigate those questions with Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) and the Valyu Search API. REA helps inspect application packages and local artifacts. Valyu retrieves the public documentation needed to interpret the APIs, formats, and behavior you encounter.

TL;DR

To reverse engineer application behavior with REA and a Search API, inspect an authorized local target, turn a concrete finding into a public technical query, retrieve the relevant documentation with Valyu, and test the explanation against that application version. Keep local observations separate from documented expectations.

We'll apply that workflow to three jobs:

Question Target Useful outcome
Where did a deleted photo go? Fossify Gallery on an Android test emulator Distinguish the app's recycle-bin behavior from permanent deletion.
Where does code you never saved live? VS Code in a separate test instance Trace an unsaved document to its backup and restoration path.
What survives an uninstall? Joplin in a disposable macOS environment Separate the application bundle from the profile holding its data.

These are hands-on walkthroughs, not reports of completed device experiments. The linked primary sources establish the documented behavior; the steps show how to investigate your selected builds. Use synthetic data throughout.

What do REA and a Search API each contribute?

REA is a CLI and MCP server for software reverse engineering. Its documented targets include native binaries, JavaScript and Electron applications, Android APKs, SQLite databases, and saved network captures. The required analysis engine depends on the target.

Valyu Search retrieves ranked source material with URLs and extracted content. In this workflow, your agent or application controls the questions and reasons over the results. That is why we're using Search rather than delegating the whole job to a report-writing service.

Suppose an APK inspection points to MediaStore.createTrashRequest. REA can help you follow the relevant code. Valyu can find Android's description of what that call requests, which API levels support it, and how it differs from createDeleteRequest.

Neither finding finishes the investigation. A method in a package does not prove the app called it when you tapped Delete. A platform API's existence does not prove your gallery uses it.

The loop is:

Observe an action in the app
  → inspect the relevant package or local artifact with REA
  → search the public API, format, or behavior with Valyu
  → formulate a specific explanation
  → test it against the same application version

Keep private artifacts out of the search query. An API name belongs in a documentation search. Your photographs, database rows, backup contents, and credentials do not.

Set up the investigation tools

You'll need an MCP-capable coding agent, a compatible Node.js runtime, Python 3.10 or later for the accompanying search helper, and a Valyu API key.

REA's runtime requirements can change. Check the published package before installing:

npm view rea-agents dist-tags.latest engines --json

Then follow the official REA setup:

npx rea-agents@latest setup

Select your client, review the proposed configuration changes, and restart the client afterward. Record the installed REA version. Repository main can describe tools that are not yet in your installed release; use the connected server's actual tool list and schemas.

Setup registers the agent integration; it does not necessarily put a standalone rea command on your shell's PATH. The terminal examples below use that command. If you do not already have it, install the CLI separately:

npm install --global rea-agents@latest
rea --help

If you use both CLI and MCP, record both versions and refresh the agent registration when you update it. Updating a global CLI does not automatically replace an existing agent registration.

The examples have different prerequisites:

  • JavaScript/Electron static inspection does not require Hopper or Ghidra.
  • Android APK inspection needs the full JDK and JADX engine specified in REA's Android guide.
  • Device inspection needs your own Android emulator and adb. REA does not install or start an emulator for you. Its ADB guide describes the read-only and device-changing operations separately.

Inspect only software you are authorized to examine. Use a disposable emulator for the phone example and a disposable account or VM for uninstall tests. Do not let an agent experiment with your daily photo library or editor profile.

Add public documentation search

For agent-driven searches, connect the Valyu MCP server at [https://mcp.valyu.ai/mcp](https://mcp.valyu.ai/mcp) using your client's remote MCP setup and sign-in flow. REA remains the local inspection tool; Valyu is the remote research tool.

For explicit, repeatable requests, use the accompanying search_docs.py. It uses Python's standard library, reads VALYU_API_KEY, and sends one request to POST https://api.valyu.ai/v1/search per invocation.

Set the key without placing its value in a command or source file. In Bash or zsh:

read -s VALYU_API_KEY
export VALYU_API_KEY
mkdir -p evidence

Paste the key and press Enter. Keep evidence/ out of version control if it will contain investigation material.

The helper sends this request body, with a query and domain list supplied at runtime:

{
  "query": "Android MediaStore createTrashRequest versus createDeleteRequest",
  "search_type": "web",
  "included_sources": ["developer.android.com"],
  "max_num_results": 5,
  "response_length": "short",
  "include_image_links": false
}

It retains each result's title, URL, source, available publication date, and content, plus the retrieval timestamp, transaction ID, and any warnings. It never reads or uploads your local application artifacts.

Searches consume credits. Review current pricing and set account or key limits before automating a large investigation. An empty successful result set means no evidence was returned for that request, not that the behavior is undocumented.

Example 1: Where do deleted photos go?

You deleted the wrong photo. Before installing a recovery utility or assuming it is gone forever, there is a more useful question: did the app move it to a recycle bin, remove a media entry, or request permanent deletion?

There is no single answer for every phone and gallery. We'll narrow the target to Fossify Gallery, whose project documents a built-in recycle bin, running on an Android emulator you control.

Start with a photo you can afford to lose

Create a PNG containing a visible label such as DAY28-PHOTO-TEST. Use no personal photograph or location metadata. Install an official gallery build in the emulator, copy the PNG into a test album, and record:

  • The gallery version, APK digest, and Android API level.
  • Whether its recycle bin is enabled.
  • The photo's initial location and SHA-256 digest.
  • Whether cloud synchronization or device backup is involved. Leave both out of this local experiment.

With the emulator running, these documented REA commands identify the target and acquire its package. Substitute the serial returned by list-adb-devices; emulator-5554 is an example:

rea list-adb-devices
rea inspect-adb-device emulator-5554
rea inspect-adb-package emulator-5554 org.fossify.gallery
rea pull-adb-package emulator-5554 org.fossify.gallery \
  --output-directory "$PWD/evidence/gallery-package"

Use a fresh output destination. REA package acquisition refuses an existing destination rather than silently replacing evidence. Follow the returned host-local APK path for the next step; do not confuse it with a device path.

For this walkthrough, prefer an official standalone APK. ADB acquisition can retrieve an installed split-APK set, but REA's documented static APK workflow does not merge splits or analyze an Android App Bundle as one application. Missing code in a base APK does not establish that the installed app lacks that feature.

Ask the agent:

Use REA to inspect the acquired Fossify Gallery APK.
Trace the entry point for deleting a photo with the recycle bin enabled.
Identify the file operations, database changes, or platform requests involved.
Return the actual class and method names, evidence locations, and unresolved calls.
Do not launch the app, change permissions, or delete anything.

If working in the terminal, rea inspect-android-package /absolute/path/to/gallery.apk starts package inspection. Discover class and method names before selecting them. Decompiled names can differ between builds; a guessed class called RecycleBinManager is not evidence.

Research the operation you actually find

Android documents two distinct batch operations on Android 11 and later: createTrashRequest requests moving items into or out of trash, while createDeleteRequest requests immediate permanent deletion without first putting them in trash. User-consent requirements depend on the operation and app privileges.

Retrieve that context with:

python3 search_docs.py \
  "Android MediaStore createTrashRequest versus createDeleteRequest user consent" \
  developer.android.com > evidence/photo-docs.json

That gives you platform semantics to compare with the trace. It does not establish that Fossify uses either method. The gallery may implement its own recycle-bin storage. Follow the code you have, then research its actual calls.

Run delete, restore, and permanent delete separately

In the emulator, perform each action manually and record the state after it:

Action What to check
Move the test photo to the recycle bin Original path, any observed destination, media entry, and app metadata.
Restore it The readable file, restored location, and whether its digest matches the original.
Permanently delete a fresh test copy The exact operation invoked and the accessible artifacts remaining afterward.

Use REA's authorized device inspection where it can read the relevant paths. An Android permission denial is a limit on the observation, not proof that the directory is empty. Do not bypass the sandbox just to complete the table.

The useful outcome is an explanation of this gallery's deletion path and a tested restore through its supported recycle bin. A leftover thumbnail would be a separate artifact, not proof that the full-resolution original is recoverable. A file missing from accessible paths would not prove that every physical storage block has been erased.

For your own deleted photos, check the gallery's supported trash and backup options first. This walkthrough is not a promise of forensic recovery.

Example 2: Where does VS Code keep a document you never saved?

An untitled tab has no ordinary filename to reopen. Yet VS Code can bring it back after you quit. The persistence mechanism is Hot Exit, which remembers unsaved changes.

Auto Save writes changes automatically under configured conditions. Local history records file versions under its own settings. Those features are related, but they do not answer the same question.

Make a separate editor instance

If the code CLI is installed, start a new instance with dedicated user-data and extension directories:

Use a standard, non-portable installation. In VS Code Portable Mode, the portable data directory overrides these directory flags, so they would not provide the separation this test requires. Leave Settings Sync disconnected in the test instance.

LAB="$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/day28-code.XXXXXX")"
code --new-window \
  --user-data-dir "$LAB/user-data" \
  --extensions-dir "$LAB/extensions" \
  --disable-extensions

Keep that terminal open so $LAB remains available. In the test instance, turn Auto Save off and confirm Hot Exit is enabled. Open an untitled text document and type DAY28-UNSAVED-7e91 followed by a few lines. Do not save it. Allow the editor to create its backup, then quit that instance normally. Do not use your real session or force-kill an editor containing work you care about.

Ask REA to inspect the packaged JavaScript directory of the editor build you installed:

Trace unsaved working-copy backup and restoration in this VS Code package.
Find how the configured user-data directory affects backup paths.
Follow writes and reads relevant to an untitled text document.
Show evidence locations and distinguish static call paths from observed execution.
Do not modify the package or open my normal editor profile.

REA's analyze-javascript-application command accepts an application directory or supported ASAR target. Use the actual location for your build rather than assuming every Electron app has the same package layout.

Connect the backup path to the documented behavior 

python3 search_docs.py \
  "VS Code Hot Exit untitled unsaved changes Backups user-data-dir versus Auto Save" \
  code.visualstudio.com > evidence/unsaved-docs.json

Microsoft's Hot Exit documentation lists backup directories for standard installations, including $HOME/Library/Application Support/Code/Backups on macOS. Our test deliberately uses a separate user-data directory, so inspect that instance's location instead of searching your normal profile.

On a copy of the test backup, find the marker and inspect the surrounding record. Let the observed format determine how you separate metadata from document text. Do not assume that every backup is a plain-text file with an interchangeable first line.

Then reopen the same test instance:

code --new-window \
  --user-data-dir "$LAB/user-data" \
  --extensions-dir "$LAB/extensions" \
  --disable-extensions

Compare the restored text with the fixture you typed. If you extract a text payload independently, compare that too. Matching a short marker alone is weaker evidence than recovering the entire expected document.

The decision this answers is practical: when an untitled document survives, look for an application-owned backup before assuming the content exists only in memory. Conversely, do not treat Hot Exit as a guarantee that every last keystroke survives every crash. Timing, settings, version, and failure conditions still matter.

Example 3: What happens to your data when you uninstall an app?

You remove an application, reinstall it, and your settings return. That does not automatically mean the uninstall failed. The executable and the user profile may have different lifetimes.

For a concrete target, use Joplin in a disposable macOS VM. Joplin's desktop app uses Electron, and its documented architecture stores notes, settings, and cache in a local SQLite database. Its home-directory documentation also describes data outside the application bundle.

Apple's uninstall guidance says removing an app does not remove documents or other files you created with it. It recommends an app's own uninstaller when one is provided. That is background context, not a substitute for checking the application you selected.

Follow one note and one setting

In the VM, install an official Joplin build and leave synchronization disabled. Create a note titled DAY28-UNINSTALL-TEST and change one preference. Record the application version and the actual profile location reported by that installation.

Ask the agent:

Use REA to inspect this Joplin desktop package.
Trace how it selects its profile directory and opens its local database.
Identify which relevant paths are inside the application bundle and which are outside it.
Return evidence for those paths, with any platform or configuration uncertainty.
Do not read unrelated profiles, remove files, or run an uninstall operation.

Quit the app completely and make a consistent copy of the whole test profile. Do not copy only a live SQLite main file while ignoring its write-ahead log. Inspect the copied database schema first; then locate the synthetic note using the schema you actually found.

This read-only Python example lists tables without dumping note contents. Supply the real path to your copied database:

from pathlib import Path
import sqlite3
import sys

database = Path(sys.argv[1]).resolve(strict=True)
connection = sqlite3.connect(database.as_uri() + "?mode=ro", uri=True)
try:
    rows = connection.execute(
        "SELECT name FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type = 'table' ORDER BY name"
    )
    for (name,) in rows:
        print(name)
finally:
    connection.close()

Save it as list_tables.py and run python3 list_tables.py /absolute/path/to/copied-database.sqlite. REA's SQLite inspection is another option when its provider and required runtime are available.

Research the uninstall boundary, then test it 

python3 search_docs.py \
  "macOS uninstall application documents remain Joplin desktop profile local database" \
  support.apple.com joplinapp.org > evidence/uninstall-docs.json

Follow the documented uninstall procedure inside the VM only. Record the state before reinstalling anything: is the application bundle gone, does the profile remain, and can a read-only copy still provide the synthetic note?

Only afterward reinstall and observe what happens. Keeping sync disabled prevents a server from quietly restoring the note and confusing the local-storage test. Account for OS restore or backup mechanisms too if they are enabled.

The outcome to establish is whether that uninstall removes the program, its profile, both, or a user-selected subset. If data remains, show the actual path and its role. Do not label it a security flaw merely because it persists.

Platform matters here. Android's storage documentation distinguishes app-specific files, which are removed on uninstall, from shared media, which is not. A result from one desktop app cannot answer what every phone app does.

Keep an evidence record, not just an explanation

A readable story is useful. A readable story attached to the wrong version is a trap.

For each example, record the app version, OS version, relevant settings, artifact digests, exact action, observation time, and public source URLs. Separate three kinds of statement:

Statement What it establishes
"Android documents this API as a trash request." The documented contract for that platform API.
"This APK contains a method that invokes it." A static implementation finding, subject to analysis coverage.
"This action produced this artifact in the test." An observation in that recorded environment.

Those statements can support one another, but none should silently replace the others.

Treat source pages, decompiled strings, logs, and filenames as untrusted data. They can contain instructions that have nothing to do with your investigation. They do not authorize the agent to install software, change permissions, delete files, or upload local material.

REA's analysis runs locally, but its results become available to the agent that called it. That agent's provider has its own data policy. Local inspection is not a promise that every downstream component is offline.

Frequently asked questions

What is Reverse Engineer Anything?

Reverse Engineer Anything, or REA, is an open-source CLI and MCP server that connects agents to tools for inspecting software artifacts and behavior. Its supported workflows include JavaScript/Electron, Android APK, native-binary, and other forms of analysis. Providers, prerequisites, and available tools depend on the installed version and target.

Why use a Search API for reverse engineering?

A Search API helps resolve public technical context around findings: API semantics, file-format documentation, platform restrictions, and version-specific discussions. It complements local inspection. Search results cannot establish that a particular code path executed or that an inaccessible artifact does not exist.

Can REA recover permanently deleted photos?

This article makes no such promise. A gallery's supported recycle-bin restore is different from forensic recovery after permanent deletion. Recoverability depends on the application, storage system, encryption, backups, and what has happened since deletion. A thumbnail or metadata entry is not the original photograph.

Do these examples require a closed-source application?

No. Open-source targets make it easier to check your interpretation afterward. Inspecting a packaged build remains a useful exercise because it exposes the artifact users actually installed. Be explicit about when you consult source code, and do not present an existing documented feature as a newly discovered secret.

Follow the action past the screen

"Deleted," "unsaved," and "uninstalled" describe user-facing states. To understand the data, follow the operation into the files, metadata, and storage boundaries behind it.

REA helps you inspect that path. Valyu helps you find the public technical material that explains it. A controlled test tells you whether your explanation fits the application in front of you.

Pick one of the three examples, keep the scope small, and record enough detail for someone else to check it. If you share a result, include the version and the evidence. "I found a backup" is useful. "Nothing is ever really deleted" is a much bigger claim.

articles.title: Stop Calling form.submit(). Use requestSubmit() Instead.
articles.description: A Save button living outside the <form> tag, wired to form.submit(), looks like it works — until a blank required field sails through and the page does a full reload your fetch handler never saw coming. requestSubmit() is the method that actually clicks the button for you.
articles.body_html:
The bug report said "the modal saves blank data sometimes." Not always — just sometimes, and only for one field: the user's email. QA could reproduce it maybe one click in five, and only if they clicked Save fast, before the field had a chance to go red.

Here's the part that should have been impossible: the input had required on it. HTML form validation is supposed to catch an empty required field before anything goes anywhere. And yet, once in a while, it didn't — the page would flash white for a quarter second, like it had just reloaded, and the record would land in the database with an empty string where the email should be.

It had reloaded. That was the whole bug, once you knew to look for it.

The button that lived outside the form

The modal in question followed a pattern you've probably built yourself: the form fields sit in the body of the dialog, but the "Cancel" / "Save" buttons live in a shared footer component that's reused across every modal in the app — rendered as a sibling, not a child, of the <form> element.

<form id="profile-form">
  <input name="email" type="email" required />
  <!-- more fields -->
</form>

<!-- the footer is a separate component, outside the form -->
<div class="modal-footer">
  <button type="button" id="cancel-btn">Cancel</button>
  <button type="button" id="save-btn">Save</button>
</div>

You can't put a type="submit" button outside a <form> and have it submit that form just by proximity — the DOM doesn't work that way. So whoever wired this up reached for the obvious-looking fix: give the form an id, grab a reference to it, and submit it from the button's click handler.

document.getElementById("profile-form").addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  saveProfile(new FormData(e.target)); // a fetch() call
});

document.getElementById("save-btn").addEventListener("click", () => {
  document.getElementById("profile-form").submit();
});

This reads like it should work. It even looks like it works most of the time — click Save with a filled-in form, and the profile saves. The bug only shows up on the path nobody tests by hand: clicking Save on an invalid form, fast, before you've noticed the field is empty.

Before you scroll: what do you think form.submit() actually skips? It's not a trick question — the answer is in the method's own name, once you say it out loud.

.submit() doesn't click anything — it just submits

form.submit() is one of the oldest methods on the DOM, older than addEventListener itself, and it does exactly what it says: it submits the form, as raw HTTP, right now. What it does not do is simulate a user clicking a submit button — and that distinction is the entire bug.

Clicking a real <button type="submit"> triggers a sequence: the browser runs the form's constraint validation (required, pattern, type="email", minlength, all of it); if anything fails, the browser blocks the submission and shows the native "Please fill out this field" bubble; only if everything passes does it fire a cancelable submit event, which is what your addEventListener("submit", ...) handler is listening for.

form.submit() skips every step of that. No validation runs. No submit event fires. The form just submits — as a real, browser-driven navigation to its action URL, using its method — which is exactly the "page flash" QA saw. The saveProfile fetch call never ran, because the event it's attached to never fired. The browser did its own, uncontrolled submission underneath your SPA's feet.

That's not a bug in .submit(). It's the method doing its one job — bypass everything and submit — which happens to be the one job you never actually wanted.

The fix is a different method, not a different pattern

requestSubmit() exists for precisely this situation: you need to trigger a form's submission from code, and you want it to behave exactly like clicking a real submit button would — because that's literally what it does.

document.getElementById("save-btn").addEventListener("click", () => {
  document.getElementById("profile-form").requestSubmit();
});

One word changed. The behavior is now correct: an empty email field blocks submission and shows the native validation bubble, a filled one runs constraint validation, passes, and fires a real submit event — which your existing e.preventDefault() handler catches, exactly as if someone had clicked a submit button that was actually inside the form.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

requestSubmit() also takes an optional argument: a specific <button> to submit "as." Pass the actual button that was clicked, and the submission carries that button's name/value pair and honors its formaction / formmethod overrides — the same as a real click would, if you have more than one submit button with different behavior (a "Save" vs. "Save and publish," say).

form.requestSubmit(saveAndPublishButton);

One sharp edge here, and it's the kind that only shows up once: the button you pass has to actually be a submit button associated with that form — a descendant of it, or linked via form="profile-form". Pass a type="button" that isn't a submit button at all, and requestSubmit() throws immediately; pass a real submit button that belongs to a different form, and it throws too, just under a different error name. Either way it's a loud, synchronous failure, not a silent no-op — that's louder than .submit() ever gave you, and louder is better here: you find out in testing, not from a QA ticket three sprints later.

The part worth double-checking: is this safe to ship everywhere?

Yes, and that's worth saying plainly, because plenty of the newer form and DOM APIs aren't. requestSubmit() shipped in Chrome in 2019 and Firefox followed in 2020 — Safari was the holdout, catching up in Safari 16 in September 2022, which is the point it became Baseline: available in every evergreen browser, no flag and no polyfill required. There's no fallback section needed in this post, which is rarer than it should be.

The only real caveat is the one most people hit the opposite way: .submit() still exists, does nothing wrong by its own definition, and will keep compiling and "working" forever — nothing errors, nothing warns, your linter stays silent. The only signal you get that you reached for the wrong method is a user complaint that doesn't reproduce consistently, which is exactly the shape of bug that's expensive to track down and cheap to prevent.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The fix here was one word. Finding it meant noticing that "the page flashed and reloaded" is .submit()'s actual, documented behavior wearing a disguise — not a flaky bug, not a race condition, just a method doing precisely what it says and nothing you asked for. Anywhere your code calls .submit() to trigger a form from outside it — a footer button, a keyboard shortcut, a wizard's "Next" step — that's requestSubmit()'s job, not .submit()'s.

Have you shipped a "phantom reload" bug like this one? What gave it away first — the validation that didn't run, or the request that never showed up in the network tab?
